opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a distinction we think about a lot, because it really changes what you learn about a model.

With coarse-grained action recognition, think of a benchmark like Kinetics. A lot of the classes can be recognized from a single frame, or from the scene context. If you see a swimming pool and someone in the water, you can guess "swimming" with pretty high confidence without understanding any motion. So these benchmarks are often appearance-heavy. A strong image model, applied frame by frame and averaged, can do surprisingly well on them. That tells you the model has good semantic, object-level, and scene-level features. It doesn't necessarily tell you it understands what's happening over time.

Fine-grained temporal recognition is a different story. The canonical example is Something-Something v2. The classes are things like "pushing something from left to right" versus "pushing something from right to left," or "pretending to put something into something" versus actually putting it in. The objects and the scene are basically the same across those classes. The only thing that distinguishes them is the motion and the temporal ordering. You can't solve it from a single frame. If you shuffle the frames or reverse them, the label changes. Datasets like Diving-48 are similar: the backgrounds are all the same diving venues, and what matters is the precise sequence of twists and somersaults.

So when we evaluate a video model, especially a self-supervised one like V-JEPA, we deliberately look at both. We typically use a frozen backbone with a lightweight attentive probe on top, so we're measuring the quality of the representation itself rather than how well you can fine-tune. Then we compare performance on the appearance-centric tasks against the motion-centric ones.

What you tend to see is quite revealing. Image-pretrained models, or models trained with heavy image-text alignment, are very strong on Kinetics-style tasks but fall off on Something-Something. Models trained to predict in a learned representation space over time, with masking that spans space and time, do much better on the temporal side. That's the gap we care about, because if the goal is a model that understands and eventually predicts how the world evolves, getting the appearance right is only half of it. You need the representation to encode dynamics.

There are a few sanity checks you can layer on as well. You can test how sensitive the model is to frame order. You can vary the number of frames or the temporal stride and see whether performance actually depends on temporal context. And you can look at tasks like action anticipation, where you have to predict what comes next. Taken together, those give you a much clearer picture than a single top-1 number on one benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response says fine-grained classes cannot be solved from a single frame, but does not establish that one or two frames are insufficient.

r002.rationale: It says many coarse-grained classes can be recognized from a single frame or scene context, using visual appearance cues.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that a lot of the classic action recognition benchmarks, something like Kinetics, are really appearance benchmarks in disguise. If you look at a single frame and you see a basketball hoop and someone in a jersey, you can pretty much guess "playing basketball." You don't actually need to understand the motion. So a lot of models that do well there are essentially very good image models that happen to average over a few frames.

Fine-grained temporal recognition is the setting where that shortcut stops working. The canonical example is Something-Something v2, where the categories are things like "pushing something from left to right" versus "pushing something from right to left," or "pretending to pick something up" versus actually picking it up. The objects and the background are identical across classes, so the only signal is how things change over time, and often the ordering of frames matters. If you shuffle the frames, a good model should fall apart, and if it doesn't, that's a sign it was never really using the temporal information.

So when we evaluate a video model, we try to look at both. The coarse benchmarks tell you whether the representation captures appearance and semantics, which is still important. The fine-grained ones tell you whether the model has actually learned something about dynamics, about motion and causality, rather than just a bag of frames. And for us that distinction matters a lot, because the whole point of learning from video rather than images is to capture that temporal structure. If a video model only wins on the appearance-heavy benchmarks, you haven't really gained anything over a strong image encoder.

r001.rationale: The response says fine-grained classes depend on changes over time and frame ordering, but does not state that they cannot be identified from just one or two frames.

r002.rationale: It says appearance-heavy benchmarks such as Kinetics can often be guessed from a single frame, giving a hoop and jersey as visual cues, and describes models that average a few frames.

astra-6.text:
The distinction is really how much you need to understand about how the scene evolves over time. For coarse-grained action recognition, you might want to identify that someone is playing basketball. You can often get pretty far from a single frame: you see the court, the ball, and the players, and that gives you a strong clue.

Fine-grained temporal recognition asks you to distinguish actions that might look very similar in individual frames. Is someone picking an object up or putting it down? Are they opening something or closing it? The objects and the setting can be identical, so you need to track what changes and in what order.

When evaluating a video model, that distinction matters because doing well on an action-recognition benchmark doesn’t necessarily mean the model understands motion. We also want tasks where the temporal information is essential to getting the answer right.

r001.rationale: It explains that fine-grained actions can look alike in individual frames and require tracking what changes and in what order, so a frame alone cannot distinguish them.

r002.rationale: It says coarse-grained actions such as playing basketball can often be inferred from a single frame using cues like the court, ball, and players.

sol-6.1.text:
The key distinction is how much you need to understand about the ordering of events. For coarse-grained action recognition, you might be asked whether someone is playing basketball or swimming. Often, a single frame gives you a lot of information: you can recognize the court, the ball, or the pool without really understanding the motion.

Fine-grained temporal recognition asks you to distinguish actions that can look very similar in individual frames. Is someone picking something up or putting it down? Are they opening something or closing it? You need to see how the scene changes over time, and the order of the frames matters.

So, when evaluating a video model, we want tasks where appearance alone isn’t enough. Strong performance on a coarse action-recognition benchmark doesn’t necessarily tell us that the model has learned those temporal relationships.

r001.rationale: The response says fine-grained actions can look similar in individual frames and that distinguishing them requires seeing how the scene changes over time, which conveys that one or two frames alone are insufficient.

r002.rationale: It explains that coarse-grained actions such as basketball or swimming can often be recognized from a single frame using visual cues like a court, ball, or pool.
